nodes.name: Diatoms (Aulacoseira)
nodes.desc: Microscopic glassy algae that bloom in and under the ice. Over 400 diatom species live in Baikal, and about half are found nowhere else.

nodes.name: Taiga shore forest
nodes.desc: Forest and shrub cover around the lake that feeds and shelters shore animals such as bears and sables.

nodes.name: Epischura copepod
nodes.desc: An endemic copepod that makes up most of the zooplankton biomass and filters the open water. Golomyanka and seals eat it.

nodes.name: Pelagic amphipod
nodes.desc: An open-water amphipod, often compared to krill. Golomyanka and Baikal seals eat it.

nodes.name: Baikal sponges
nodes.desc: Endemic filter feeders found from shallows to over 500 m deep. Most are green from symbiotic algae in their tissue.

nodes.name: Baikal amphipods
nodes.desc: A very diverse endemic group. Some are mostly carnivorous, others eat detritus, and the high oxygen of the lake is linked to the giant size of some.

nodes.name: Golomyanka (oilfish)
nodes.desc: Translucent, live-bearing deep-water fish and the most numerous fish in the lake. They rise toward the surface at night to feed on copepods and amphipods.

nodes.name: Baikal sculpins
nodes.desc: Small endemic bottom and open-water fish. Baikal seals eat them, especially in autumn.

nodes.name: Omul
nodes.desc: An endemic whitefish and the lake's main commercial fish. It eats zooplankton, algae and some small fish, and spawns in the rivers feeding the lake.

nodes.name: Osprey
nodes.desc: A fish-eating bird of prey that hunts in shallow water along the shore.

nodes.name: White-tailed eagle
nodes.desc: A large raptor that takes fish and, per the seal article, can prey on seal pups that leave their dens.

nodes.name: Sable
nodes.desc: A forest-dwelling marten of the taiga. It can take seal pups that leave their ice dens.

nodes.name: Baikal seal (nerpa)
nodes.desc: The only seal living entirely in fresh water. Golomyanka make up most of its diet, and it digs breathing holes and dens in the ice.

nodes.name: Brown bear
nodes.desc: Roams the taiga shore. It is the only known natural predator of adult Baikal seals, though attacks are thought to be rare.

nodes.name: Winter ice
nodes.desc: The lake is frozen for about four to five months, and the clear ice lets light in for under-ice algae. Seals dig dens in it.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light drives algae growth, especially through clear winter ice and in the open summer water.

nodes.name: Deep oxygenated water
nodes.desc: Unlike many deep lakes, Baikal keeps oxygen at depth, which lets animals live throughout the water column.

nodes.name: Dissolved nutrients
nodes.desc: River inflow and recycled nutrients feed algal growth in the lake.

nodes.name: Bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead algae, plankton and animals, returning nutrients to the water.
